newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson could testify by late next week.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson could testify by late next week.

text.p: O.J. Simpson, who never took the witness stand in his murder trial, could begin testifying at his wrongful death civil trial by late next week, according to a witness list submitted on Friday.
Simpson, a former athlete, actor and TV pitchman, was acquitted in October of last year of murdering his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman.

The lineup of upcoming witnesses was released by the plaintiffs on the same day a woman alternate juror was dismissed after Simpson's lead attorney complained that she had been dozing off during testimony.
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki announced the removal of the 18-year-old woman, who is white, to the remaining jurors, telling them: "Do not speculate as to the reason why."

Attorneys for relatives of the two murder victims said on Friday they had fewer than 10 more witnesses to call before they get to Simpson. They estimated the others, including limousine driver Allan Park and former Simpson houseguest Kato Kaelin, would be through testifying by next Thursday, the earliest Simpson might be called.

But there was no guarantee everything would go according to plan. Simpson is embroiled in legal battles on two fronts including a suburban Orange County courtroom where trial began this week in his fight to regain full custody of his two young children from the parents of his slain ex-wife, and his lead defence attorney, Robert Baker, said his client was committed to attending the child-custody trial.

Baker said it would take a court order to get Simpson to testify in Santa Monica before the Orange County proceedings have ended. "If the court orders him to be here, he'll be here," he said. "Otherwise he'll be in Orange County."

Simpson had the right to refuse to testify during his criminal trial, which ended on Oct. 3, 1995, with his acquittal on double-murder charges. But under the rules of civil procedure he can be forced to take the stand or forfeit his case, which could cost him millions of dollars in damages.

Simpson's testimony was expected to take up to five days and he can be called again during the defence portion of the case. Among those scheduled to take the stand before Simpson are several scientific and domestic violence witnesses.

Gary Sims, a California Department of Justice DNA expert who testified for a second day on Friday, conceded under cross-examination by Simpson attorney Robert Blasier that contamination is possible in DNA testing, but he said there was no evidence that happened in this case.
Simpson's attorneys contend that blood and DNA evidence in the case was mishandled, contaminated and in some cases planted by police investigators.

The dismissal of the woman juror on Friday left six alternates who can be seated on the regular jury if one or more of the 12 panellists are removed. According to transcripts Baker asked that the woman be dismissed, saying "I think she has been asleep throughout a large portion of this trial."

The plaintiffs' lawyers objected and alleged that another juror, a black woman, had also been sleeping at times. But Fujisaki decided to dismiss only the white woman for now and said he would "keep an eye" on the other panellist.

During dry DNA testimony on Thursday, Fujisaki interrupted the defence cross-examination briefly and said it appeared to be putting one or more of the jurors to sleep. He ordered the panel to pay attention.
